body: Renaissance Midtown West LLC sued its former tenant, Lividini & Company, LLC, and the tenant's principal in New York County Supreme Court in November 2024, seeking rent for the balance of the lease term, enforcement of a guaranty and an order piercing the corporate veil. According to the decision, the tenant's counsel gave notice in August 2020 that the tenant was vacating, the tenant returned the keys without objection, and the landlord later signed a lease with a new tenant; the landlord acknowledged there was no further communication between the parties until it sued. Justice Lyle E. Frank granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the amended complaint in an order entered July 24, 2025.

A First Department panel of Justices Webber, Kapnick, Shulman, Pitt-Burke and Hagler unanimously affirmed on October 27, 2026. Paragraph 17(1) of the lease is a conditional limitation that lets the landlord end the lease for defaults other than nonpayment, including if the premises become "vacant or deserted," by serving a five-day notice to cure and then a three-day notice of cancellation. Citing Holy Properties v. Cole Products, the court held that the tenant's vacatur triggered its right to that notice before reentry and reletting. It rejected the landlord's argument that it meant only to collect rent, not to terminate, because taking back the keys and reletting the space were at odds with a continuing landlord-tenant relationship.

The court also held that lease paragraph 17(2) and rider paragraph 66, which the landlord invoked for unpaid amounts, apply only while the tenant remains in possession. It distinguished 622 Third Ave. Co. LLC v. Hyatt Leader Ltd., where the landlord had told the tenant that accepting the surrender was without prejudice to a claim for unpaid rent; no such allegation was made here.

The guaranty claim failed under General Obligations Law § 5-701(a)(2) because the standard-form guaranty attached to the lease was blank and unexecuted, and the landlord alleged no facts warranting leave to replead. On veil piercing, the court, citing Cortlandt Street Recovery Corp. v. Bonderman, said the doctrine is not a separate cause of action, and a bare allegation that the principal did not keep a bank account separate from the tenant's did not show domination and control used to commit a wrong against the landlord.

timeline.label: Tenant's counsel gives landlord notice that the tenant is vacating the premises
Landlord commences action in New York County Supreme Court for unpaid rent, guaranty liability and veil-piercing
Supreme Court, New York County grants tenant's motion to dismiss the amended complaint
Appellate Division, First Department unanimously affirms dismissal
